newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein says Major hindering Irish peace quest.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein says Major hindering Irish peace quest.

text.p: The IRA's Sinn Fein political wing accused British Prime Minister John Major on Thursday of frustrating the Northern Irish peace process after he said it would take more than "soft words" for them to get into talks.

In a gloomy verdict on prospects for an early breakthrough, Major said he would need to be convinced that any future Irish Republican Army truce was not just a tactical device to be jettisoned at the guerrillas' whim.
The IRA broke its 17-month ceasefire in February throwing the Anglo-Irish sponsored peace process that had limped along for nearly three years into chaos.
Britain, backed by Ireland, insists the IRA must call a new ceasefire before Sinn Fein is allowed into the all-party talks.
Sinn Fein attacked Major for sideing with pro-British Unionist politicians whom they say want preconditions for early guerrilla disarmament that could stall Sinn Fein's entry to the talks.

"Sinn Fein has been working with others in trying to bring about a situation where real and meaningful peace negotiations can take place against a background of a peaceful enviornment, and that work is on-going," spokesman Martin McGuinness told Reuters.

"I think that John Major's speech makes all of that much He described Major's remarks in parliament as "a reaffirmation of comments by David Trimble (leader of the powerful Ulster Unionist Party) that in the event of a possible new IRA ceasefire, Sinn Fein would face new terms and conditions," McGuinness said.
"I think that is undoubtedly damaging to the work that we (Sinn Fein) are doing."

Police in London have warned that dangerous months ahead could see more guerrilla bombs in mainland Britain. But the Dublin media reported this week that Sinn Fein, through private contacts, has been trying to determine how Britain would respond if the IRA reinstated its ceasefire.
Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring said in a radio interview on Wednesday that Sinn Fein could be brought into talks within weeks of a credible truce by the IRA.

Irish officials said on Thursday that Sinn Fein had "a credibility problem" because of the IRA's resurgence. They dismissed media reports of divisions between London and Dublin over the timing of Sinn Fein's admission to talks.

Ulster Unionist Party security spokesman Ken Maginnis told Reuters that the IRA must establish a permanent ceasefire and "produce a significant first tranche of weapons" before Sinn Fein could be admitted to the talks.

On October 7 IRA guerrillas set off their first bomb in Northern Ireland for two years, killing a soldier at British army headquarters south of Belfast. It followed attacks in mainland Britain and a bombing at a British army base in Germany.
